(اللَّهُ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضَ): الله is a mubtadaʾ and الذي its khabar; خلق is the ṣila; and السموات والأرض is its object. (وَأَنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً فَأَخْرَجَ بِهِ مِنَ الثَّمَراتِ رِزْقاً لَكُمْ): وأنزل is conjoined to خلق, and the agent is latent, "He," that is Allah; ومن السماء is attached to أنزل; ماء is a direct object; فأخرج is conjoined to أنزل; به is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أخرج; ومن الثمرات is a ḥāl, because it precedes what it describes, namely رزقا; رزقا is a direct object; and لكم is an adjective of رزقا. (وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ الْفُلْكَ لِتَجْرِيَ فِي الْبَحْرِ بِأَمْرِهِ): وسخر لكم الفلك is conjoined to what preceded; ولتجري: the lām is of cause, and تجري is accusative by an implied أن after the lām of cause; وفي البحر is attached to تجري; and بأمره is a ḥāl. (وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ الْأَنْهارَ): conjoined to what preceded. (وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ الشَّمْسَ وَالْقَمَرَ دائِبَيْنِ وَسَخَّرَ لَكُمُ اللَّيْلَ وَالنَّهارَ): also a conjunction; دائبين is a ḥāl from الشمس والقمر, and since they agree in word and meaning it was put in the dual, and their differing in masculine and feminine does no harm. (وَآتاكُمْ مِنْ كُلِّ ما سَأَلْتُمُوهُ): وآتاكم is also a conjunction, and it is a verb, a latent agent and a direct object; ومن كل is attached to آتاكم; ما is a relative noun annexed to كل; and سألتموه is the ṣila; ما may also be maṣdarī. (وَإِنْ تَعُدُّوا نِعْمَةَ اللَّهِ لا تُحْصُوها): The wāw is a conjunction; إن is conditional; تعدوا is the protasis and the wāw the agent; نعمة الله is the object of تعدوا; لا is negative; and تحصوها is the apodosis of إن. (إِنَّ الْإِنْسانَ لَظَلُومٌ كَفَّارٌ): A resumptive clause, set forth to stress the denial by the wrongdoing human of Allah's bounties and favours, heedless of giving thanks for them; إن and its noun; the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); ظلوم is the first khabar of إن and كفار the second khabar.

* Rhetoric:
In these verses there is a great deal of threat, menace, thundering and lightning, and we shall set out their features in order. The first: wonder expressed in the form of a question at their deeds, which have no connection with forbearance, for they exchanged the favour itself for disbelief and committed a crime against themselves and their people.
The second: the metaphor in His words «ليضلوا عن سبيل الله»; that was not their aim, but it resembles an aim because it is the inevitable result of taking rivals; so it is an explicit derivative metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya tabaʿiyya).
The third: the omission of the content of what was said in «قل لعبادي الذين آمنوا إلخ». The skilled have objected to this parsing, saying: "There is something to consider in this parsing, because the answer would then be a report from Allah the Exalted that if He says to them this saying they will comply with its requirement, so they will establish the prayer and spend; yet it has been said to them and many of them did not comply, and the report of Allah is too exalted for a breach (al-ḥalf) [Translator's note: the source prints "الحلف" (oath); "al-khulf" (breach) seems intended]. This point is what prompted many parsers to turn away from this parsing, despite its coming to mind first on the face of what is mentioned. It can be made sound by taking the general as the majority rather than as all-inclusive, and it is strengthened by two fine considerations. One is that this construction occurred only for someone described as having true faith, whose faith is lauded at the time of the command, as in this verse and others, such as the words of the Exalted «قل لعبادي يقولوا التي هي أحسن» ("Say to My servants that they should say that which is best") and «قل للمؤمنين يغضوا من أبصارهم ويحفظوا فروجهم» ("Say to the believers that they should lower their gaze and guard their private parts"). The second is the repeated occurrence of it for those described as servants of Allah, honoured by being annexed to the name of Allah the Exalted. They have said that the word 'servants' (ʿibād) does not occur in the Noble Book except as praise of the believers, especially when it is annexed to Him, the Exalted, with the annexation of honour. In sum, the one commanded in these verses is one who is on the verge of compliance and in the sphere of hastening to obedience, so the report about such people is true and veracious, either in general, if that is meant, or in the majority."
The fourth: the emphasis that made the report one of denial-addressed (inkārī) in His words «إن الإنسان لظلوم كفار». This verse includes four emphases: the first is «إن», the second is «the shifted lām or the lām of emphasis», the third is the form «ظلوم» and the fourth is the form «كفار».

dervis-irab:42-52.t:
* Vocabulary:
(مُهْطِعِينَ): hastening toward the caller. It is also said that ihṭāʿ is when you turn your gaze upon what is seen and keep looking at it without blinking. In al-Mukhtār: "The man ahṭaʿa when he stretched out his neck and lowered his head; and he ahṭaʿa in his running: he hastened." In al-Asās: "A muhṭiʿ camel: one whose neck is lowered; it is also said: it is the hastening one. He ahṭaʿa in his journey and istahṭaʿa." And he said:
تعبّدني نمر بن سعد وقد أرى ... ونمر بن سعد لي مطيع ومهطع
(Nimr ibn Saʿd enslaved me, though I see that Nimr ibn Saʿd is obedient and submissive to me.)
And another said, describing a bull:
بمستهطع رسل كأنّ زمامه ... بقيدوم رعن من رضام ممتّع
(With a hastening, easy-paced one, as though its rein were on the front of a mountain peak of lofty rocks.)
(مُقْنِعِي رُؤُسِهِمْ): iqnāʿ is raising the head and continuing to look without turning to anything else. In al-Qāmūs: "Aqnaʿahu: he satisfied him; and aqnaʿa his head: he set it upright and raised it, or he does not turn right or left and keeps his gaze level." It is also said that iqnāʿ is among the words with opposite meanings (aḍdād), meaning both raising and lowering. «مقنعي رءوسهم» means: raising them.
(الطرف): originally a verbal noun; ṭarf is also the moving of the eyelid. Jarīr said:
إن العيون التي في طرفها حور ... قتلننا ثم لم يحيين قتلانا
يصرعن ذا اللب حتى لا حراك ... وهنّ أضعف خلق الله إنسانا
(Indeed the eyes whose glance is lustrous-eyed have killed us and then did not bring our slain back to life. They fell the man of reason until he cannot move, though they are the weakest of Allah's creatures as human beings.)
(مُقَرَّنِينَ): some of them were bound together with others; their hands were bound to their feet, shackled.
(الْأَصْفادِ): fetters; it is also said: shackles. He recited a verse by Salāma ibn Jandal:
وزيد الخيل قد لاقى صفادا ... يعضّ بساعد وبعظم ساق
(And Zayd al-Khayl met with fetters that bite into the forearm and the shin bone.)
It is the plural of ṣafad. One says ṣafadahu yaṣfiduhu ṣafdan (of the pattern ḍaraba) meaning he shackled him, and ṣaffadahu with doubled middle letter for intensification. Among their sayings: "al-ṣafad ṣafad", meaning that a gift is a fetter. Figuratively: ṣaffadtuhu bi-kalāmī taṣfīdan, when you overcame him with your speech. ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm said:
فآبوا بالنهاب وبالسبايا ... وأبنا بالملوك مصفّدينا
(They returned with plunder and captives, and we returned with kings in shackles.)
(قَطِرانٍ): qaṭirān has three dialect forms: qaṭirān with fatḥa on the qāf and kasra on the ṭāʾ; qaṭrān on the pattern of sakrān; and qiṭrān with kasra on the qāf and sukūn on the ṭāʾ on the pattern of sirḥān. It is what flows from a tree called al-abhal; it is boiled, and scabby camels are smeared with it, whereupon its heat and sharpness burn away the scab and the skin, and its heat may reach the inner body. It is characteristic of it that fire catches quickly in it, and it may even be used as a lamp fuel. It is black in colour and foul in smell. The skins of the people of the Fire will be smeared with it until its coating becomes for them like sarābīl, that is, shirts, so that there combine upon them the stinging and burning of the tar, the speed of the fire in their skins, the ugly colour and the foul smell. In al-Munjid: "al-qaṭirān, al-qaṭrān and al-qiṭrān: an oily liquid obtained from some trees such as pine and cedar."

* I'rab:
(وَلا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ غافِلًا عَمَّا يَعْمَلُ الظَّالِمُونَ) The wāw is resumptive; lā is prohibitive; تحسبن is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa because of its attachment to the heavy nūn of emphasis, and it is in the position of the jussive (jazm) by the prohibitive lā; the fāʿil (agent) is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; the Glorious Name is the first direct object (mafʿūl bihi); غافلا is the second direct object; عما is attached to غافلا; and the clause يعمل الظالمون is a ṣila (relative clause).
(إِنَّما يُؤَخِّرُهُمْ لِيَوْمٍ تَشْخَصُ فِيهِ الْأَبْصارُ) This clause is also resumptive, brought to give the reason for the preceding prohibition. إنما is a restrictive particle (kāffa) and the one restricted (makfūfa); يؤخرهم is an imperfect verb with a latent agent and a direct object; ليوم is attached to يؤخرهم; the clause تشخص is an adjective (naʿt) of ليوم; فيه is attached to تشخص; and الأبصار is the fāʿil. The meaning: they do not stay fixed in their places because of the terror of what they see.
(مُهْطِعِينَ مُقْنِعِي رُؤُسِهِمْ لا يَرْتَدُّ إِلَيْهِمْ طَرْفُهُمْ وَأَفْئِدَتُهُمْ هَواءٌ) مهطعين and مقنعي رءوسهم are two ḥāls (circumstantial) from an omitted muḍāf, since the implied form is "the owners of the eyes"; or the eyes indicated their owners, so the ḥāl came from what was indicated. The clause لا يرتد إليهم طرفهم is a third ḥāl from the pronoun in مقنعي رءوسهم, and it is possible that it is resumptive. وأفئدتهم: the wāw is also for ḥāl; وأفئدتهم هواء is a mubtadaʾ and khabar, and the clause is a fourth ḥāl; it is possible that the wāw is resumptive and the clause resumptive.
(وَأَنْذِرِ النَّاسَ يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمُ الْعَذابُ) وأنذر is conjoined to the saying ولا تحسبن; الناس is the first direct object; and يوم is the second direct object, not a mafʿūl fīhi (adverbial) as one might imagine at first glance, with an omitted muḍāf, that is: "warn them of its terrors and its grave events", since there is no warning on that Day; warning takes place only in this world. The clause يأتيهم العذاب is annexed to the adverb; يأتيهم is a verb and direct object; and العذاب is a postponed fāʿil.
(فَيَقُولُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا رَبَّنا أَخِّرْنا إِلى أَجَلٍ قَرِيبٍ نُجِبْ دَعْوَتَكَ وَنَتَّبِعِ الرُّسُلَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; يقول is conjoined to يأتيهم; الذين is the fāʿil; the clause ظلموا is a ṣila; ربنا is a vocative in a genitive construct (muḍāf); أخرنا is a verb, a latent agent and a direct object; إلى أجل is attached to أخرنا; قريب is an adjective; نجب is jussive because it is the apodosis of a request, and the agent is latent, its implied form being "we"; and دعوتك is the direct object.
(أَوَلَمْ تَكُونُوا أَقْسَمْتُمْ مِنْ قَبْلُ ما لَكُمْ مِنْ زَوالٍ) The hamza is for an interrogative of rebuke and affirmation; the wāw is a conjunction; لم is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; تكونوا is a defective imperfect verb, jussive through لم, and the wāw is its subject (ism); the clause is the quoted speech (maqūl al-qawl) of an omitted "saying", that is: "so this saying is said to them in rebuke and reproach"; the clause أقسمتم is the khabar of تكونوا; ما is a negative, either Ḥijāzī or Tamīmī; لكم is a preposed khabar; من is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition; and زوال is the ism of ما, or a postponed mubtadaʾ, in position (maḥallan) genitive by من in form (lafẓan); and the clause has no grammatical position because it is the answer to an oath, and it came in the second-person form out of regard for the words أقسمتم.
(وَسَكَنْتُمْ فِي مَساكِنِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا أَنْفُسَهُمْ) وسكنتم is conjoined to أقسمتم and is a verb and agent; في مساكن is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to سكنتم; الذين is a muḍāf ilayhi of مساكن; the clause ظلموا is a ṣila; and أنفسهم is a direct object.
(وَتَبَيَّنَ لَكُمْ كَيْفَ فَعَلْنا بِهِمْ وَضَرَبْنا لَكُمُ الْأَمْثالَ) وتبين is conjoined to what precedes, and the agent is implied according to what the sentence expresses, that is, "their condition", by report and by observation; لكم is attached to تبين; كيف is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object), that is, "what deed we did to them"; you may also parse it as a ḥāl; it cannot be the fāʿil of تبين, because the interrogative noun is not governed by what precedes it and has the right of first place in the sentence; فعلنا is a verb and agent; بهم is attached to فعلنا. As for وضربنا: you may conjoin it to تبين and you may make it resumptive; ضربنا is a verb and agent; الأمثال is the direct object; and لكم is attached to ضربنا.
(وَقَدْ مَكَرُوا مَكْرَهُمْ وَعِنْدَ اللَّهِ مَكْرُهُمْ) The wāw is a conjunction; قد is a particle of affirmation; مكروا is a verb and agent; مكرهم is a mafʿūl muṭlaq; the wāw is circumstantial; عند الله is an adverb attached to an omitted preposed khabar; مكرهم is a postponed mubtadaʾ; and the hāʾ is a muḍāf ilayhi. It is either the hāʾ of the fāʿil, so that the meaning is "and their plot is recorded with Allah, so He will requite them for it with a greater plot", and it is also possible [Translator's note: the Arabic text of this passage is evidently garbled and the sentence is left unfinished and mixed with the parsing of the following verse: "and إن is negative and كان a defective past verb and مكرهم its ism and the lām is the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd), which they deserve; it comes to them from where they do not perceive"]. The first is preferable for its agreement with the hāʾ of the first مكرهم.
(وَإِنْ كانَ مَكْرُهُمْ لِتَزُولَ مِنْهُ الْجِبالُ) The wāw is a conjunction; إن is negative; كان is a defective past verb; مكرهم is its ism; the lām is the lām of denial (lām al-juḥūd); تزول is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied أن after the lām of denial; the preposition and its genitive noun are the khabar of كان; منه is attached to تزول; and الجبال is the fāʿil. The meaning is: "the mountains will not move away because of their plot." The meaning of drawing a likeness with the mountains will come in the chapter on rhetoric.
(فَلا تَحْسَبَنَّ اللَّهَ مُخْلِفَ وَعْدِهِ رُسُلَهُ) A consequential conjunction (ʿaṭf tafrīʿī) upon ولا تحسبن; lā is prohibitive; تحسبن is jussive in position by the prohibitive lā; the Glorious Name is a direct object; مخلف is the second object of تحسبن, and it is an active participle; وعده is annexed to مخلف and is the second object of مخلف; and رسله is the first object of مخلف. The original is مخلف رسله وعده, but he put "the promise" first for its importance and to announce that He never breaks a promise at all.
(إِنَّ اللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ ذُو انتِقامٍ) inna with its ism and khabar; and ذو انتقام is a second khabar for it.
(يَوْمَ تُبَدَّلُ الْأَرْضُ غَيْرَ الْأَرْضِ وَالسَّماواتُ) The adverb يوم is a badal (substitute) for يوم يأتيهم العذاب, or is attached to an omitted verb, that is, "remember the Day"; the clause تبدل is annexed to the adverb; تبدل is a passive imperfect verb; الأرض is a nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); غير الأرض is the second object of تبدل; and السموات is conjoined to الأرض, meaning that their landmarks are changed, in line with the poet's saying:
وما الناس بالناس الذين عهدتهم ... ولا الدار بالدار التي كنت تعلم
(The people are not the people you knew, nor is the abode the abode you used to know.)
In the longer works there are traditions and sayings about the changing of the earth and the heavens, and there is no harm in consulting them. (وَبَرَزُوا لِلَّهِ الْواحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ) Conjoined to تبدل, for it is a past verb with the meaning of the imperfect; لله is attached to برزوا; and الواحد القهار are two adjectives of Allah. (وَتَرَى الْمُجْرِمِينَ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُقَرَّنِينَ فِي الْأَصْفادِ) Also conjoined to تبدل; المجرمين is the direct object; the seeing here is seeing with the eye, that is, you see them with the sight of the eye; يومئذ is an adverb to which another adverb is annexed, attached to تراهم [Translator's note: the source has «تراهم» although the verb in the verse is «ترى»]; مقرنين is a ḥāl from المجرمين; and في الأصفاد is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to مقرنين, or to an omitted ḥāl. (سَرابِيلُهُمْ مِنْ قَطِرانٍ) This clause is a second ḥāl or a resumptive clause; سرابيلهم is a mubtadaʾ and من قطران is its khabar. (وَتَغْشى وُجُوهَهُمُ النَّارُ) Conjoined to the circumstantial clause; تغشى is an imperfect verb; وجوهم [sic] is a preposed direct object; and النار is a postponed fāʿil. (لِيَجْزِيَ اللَّهُ كُلَّ نَفْسٍ ما كَسَبَتْ) The lām is the lām of reason; يجزي is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied أن after the lām of reason; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to برزوا; the Glorious Name is the fāʿil; كل نفس is the direct object; and in ما كسبت, ما is the second object and the clause كسبت is a ṣila. (إِنَّ اللَّهَ سَرِيعُ الْحِسابِ) inna with its ism and khabar; the clause is explanatory of cause and has no grammatical position. (هذا بَلاغٌ لِلنَّاسِ وَلِيُنْذَرُوا بِهِ) هذا is a mubtadaʾ; بلاغ is the khabar; للناس is an adjective; ولينذروا is conjoined to an omitted element, that is, "so that they may be advised and be warned"; and به is attached to ينذروا.
(وَلِيَعْلَمُوا أَنَّما هُوَ إِلهٌ واحِدٌ وَلِيَذَّكَّرَ أُولُوا الْأَلْبابِ) وليعلموا is conjoined to لينذروا; إنما is kāffa and makfūfa, and it takes the place of the two objects of يعلموا; هو is a mubtadaʾ; إله is the khabar; واحد is an adjective; وليذكر is conjoined to what precedes; and أولو الألباب is the fāʿil.

* Rhetoric:
The allegorical metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-tamthīliyya) in His words «وإن كان مكرهم لتزول منه الجبال»: by His words لتزول منه الجبال He likened their plot, because of its magnitude, severity, their cleverness in it and their reaching the utmost of it; and He likened His law, His verses and what He sent down to His Prophet of lofty teachings and clear proofs, likened them to the mountains in their firmness and their fixity in the souls of those who believe in them and hold fast to their hems. It is among the finest and most beautiful metaphors, and its splendour increases in that the plot prepared to remove the mountains issues from a hollow people in whom there is no benefit and who have no strength; in their fickleness and lightness they are most like air, since He said before that «وأفئدتهم هواء». Hawāʾ is emptiness and void that no bodies have filled; it was used to describe the heart, so it is said "a heart of hawāʾ" when one is a coward, timid, with no strength or boldness in his heart. It is also said of the fool that his heart is hawāʾ. Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā said, describing his she-camel:
كأن الرجل منها فوق صعل ... من الظلمان جؤجؤه هواء
(As if the saddle upon her were upon a small-headed male ostrich whose breast is hollow.)
Al-Saʿl: one whose head is bare of hair, or small-headed; al-ẓulmān is the plural of ẓalīm, the male ostrich; al-juʾjuʾ is the chest. He made its chest empty so that it would be faster in going to its food; and the ostrich is proverbial for cowardice, fear and foolishness.
And Ḥassān ibn Thābit said, satirising Abū Sufyān before his conversion to Islam:
ألا أبلغ أبا سفيان عني ... فأنت مجوف نخب هواء
بأن سيوفنا تركت عبيدا ... وعبد الدار سادتها الإماء
هجوت محمدا فأجبت عنه ... وعند الله في ذاك الجزاء
أتهجوه ولست له بكفء ... فشركما لخيركما الفداء
أمن يهجو رسول الله منكم ... ويمدحه وينصره سواء
فإن أبي ووالده وعرضي ... لعرض محمد فيكم وقاء
(Tell Abū Sufyān from me: you are hollow, faint-hearted, empty, that our swords have left ʿUbayd, and the maidservants are the masters of ʿAbd al-Dār. You satirised Muḥammad and I answered on his behalf, and with Allah lies the reward for that. Do you satirise him when you are no match for him? May the worse of you be the ransom of the better of you. Is he among you who satirises the Messenger of Allah, and he who praises and supports him, equal? Truly my father, his father and my honour are a shield for the honour of Muḥammad against you.)
Al-mujawwaf, al-nakhib and al-hawāʾ: empty of belly, or empty of heart of intellect and courage. In modern times Shawqī glanced at this meaning and borrowed it to describe the maidens, saying:
فاتقوا الله في قلوب العذارى ... فالعذارى قلوبهن هواء
(Fear Allah concerning the hearts of the maidens, for the maidens' hearts are hawāʾ.)

* Benefits:
The meaning of "the day the earth is changed into other than the earth":
We transmit to you the gist of the words of Imam al-Rāzī on the words of the Exalted «يوم تبدل الأرض غير الأرض» to the end of the verse, because of its importance, and then we follow these words with remarks no less important. Al-Rāzī said:
"Know that tabdīl (change) admits of two senses. The first is that the earth remains and its attribute is exchanged for another attribute. The second is that the essence perishes and a second essence comes into being. The proof that the use of tabdīl to mean a change in attribute is permissible is that one says 'I changed the ring into a seal ring (khātam)' when you fashioned it into a seal ring and thereby moved it from one shape to another; and from this is His saying «فأولئك يبدل الله سيئاتهم حسنات», and one says 'I changed my shirt into a cloak (jubba)', that is, I moved the thing from one attribute to another, and one says 'Zayd changed' when his conditions changed. As for the mention of tabdīl when the substitution occurs in the essence, it is like your saying 'I exchanged the dirham for dinars', and from it is His saying «بدلناهم جلودا غيرها» and His saying «وبدلناهم بجنتيهم جنتين». When you know that the word admits each of these two concepts, there are two views on the verse:
The first: what is meant is a change of attribute, not a change of essence...." [Translator's note: the ellipsis is in the source, which omits the intervening text.] "And His words والسموات mean: and the heavens are changed by the scattering of their stars, their splitting open, the folding up of their sun and the eclipse of their moon and their being rolled up; at one time they are like molten metal and at another like red oil.
The second view: that what is meant is a change of essence. Ibn Masʿūd said: it will be exchanged for an earth like pure white silver, upon which no blood has been shed and upon which no sin has been committed." End of al-Rāzī's words.
The philosopher Shaykh ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn ibn al-Nafīs, in his treatise with which he countered the treatise Ḥayy ibn Yaqẓān by Ibn Ṭufayl, explained the ruin of this abode, the corruption of this world and the appearance of the signs, saying, in summary of what he meant: Since it is established that the inclination of the sun toward the north and the south constantly diminishes, then when this inclination ceases or nears cessation, the sun comes to stand continually over the equator or near it; thereby an exceedingly intense heat arises, and in the regions of great latitude an excessive cold arises, so that temperaments are corrupted, hearts weaken, sudden death increases, characters worsen, so that dealings are corrupted, evils and quarrels increase, wars and strife multiply, the wicked come to the fore and minds are corrupted, and through their corruption people recede from accepting the sciences and wisdom -- until he says: "If the loss of the sun's inclination lasts for a time, the departure from moderation becomes excessive, until it corrupts the temperaments of animals and plants, and from that the Resurrection would come about." End of the words of Ibn al-Nafīs.

dervis-irab:35-41.t:
* Vocabulary:
(وَاجْنُبْنِي): The people of the Hijaz say jannabanī sharrahu (with doubling), and the people of Najd say janabanī and ajnabanī. The meaning is "keep us and make us steadfast in avoiding their worship." One says janabahu al-sharr and ajnabahu iyyāhu, in the triliteral and quadriliteral forms, which is the dialect of Najd, and jannabahu iyyāhu (with doubling), which is the dialect of the Hijaz; it means "to prevent," and its origin is from al-jānib ("the side"). Al-Rāghib said: "His words, the Exalted, «وأجنبني وبني» are from janabtuhu ʿan kadhā, meaning 'I kept him far from it'; it is also said to be from janabtu al-faras ('I led the horse alongside'), as if he asked Him to keep him far from the side of polytheism by kindnesses from Him and hidden means; and «أن نعبد» is on the omission of the preposition, meaning 'from worshipping' (ʿan an naʿbuda)." In al-Qāmūs:
"Al-janab (with vowels) is that a horse is led alongside another horse in a race, and when the mount tires, one shifts to the one led alongside." In al-Miṣbāḥ: "janabtu al-rajula al-sharr junūban, of the pattern qaʿada, means 'I kept it away from him,' and janabtuhu with the heavy form is for intensification." In al-Mukhtār: janabahu al-shayʾ, of the pattern naṣara, and jannabahu al-shayʾ tajnīban in the same sense, that is, "he removed it from him," and from it is the saying of the Exalted:
«واجنبني وبنيّ أن نعبد الأصنام». Abū ʿAlī said: One says janabtu fulānan al-khayr, meaning "I removed him from it," and also jannabtuhu in the heavy form. Abū Naṣr said: the light form is better. Allah said: «وأجنبني وبنيّ أن نعبد الأصنام».
(تَهْوِي إِلَيْهِمْ): It inclines, yearns and flies with longing towards them. Its origin is that it is made transitive with lām, but it is made transitive with ilā because it includes the meaning of "inclines." He says in al-Asās:
hawā ilā al-jabal and hawā al-jabal means "he climbed it" (hawiyyan). Abū Bakr al-Hudhalī said, describing Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:
وإذا رميت به الفجاج رأيته ... يهوى مخارمها هوي الأجدل
("When you hurl him into the wide roads, you see him plunge through their mountain passes like the plunge of the falcon.")
That is: when you cast him into the regions of branching places, you see him plunging through their passes, meaning hastening along their narrow paths like the plunge of the falcon (al-ajdal), which is the hawk, that is, like its speed in flight.

* I'rab:
(وَإِذْ قالَ إِبْراهِيمُ رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَذَا الْبَلَدَ آمِناً): إذ is an adverbial of past time attached to "remember" (udhkur), and the clause قال is annexed to the adverbial; ابراهيم is the agent; رب is a vocative with the vocative particle omitted, annexed to the omitted yāʾ of the first-person speaker; اجعل is a verb of supplication and its agent is latent, its implied form being "You"; هذا is its first object; البلد is a badal of the demonstrative; and آمنا is a second direct object. (وَاجْنُبْنِي وَبَنِيَّ أَنْ نَعْبُدَ الْأَصْنامَ): واجنبني is a verb of supplication, the nūn is the protective nūn and the yāʾ is its object; وبني is conjoined to the yāʾ or is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment); أن نعبد: أن and what follows are in the interpretation of a maṣdar, accusative by removal of the preposition, as al-Rāghib said, that is "from worshipping" (ʿan an naʿbuda), and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to اجنبني; and الأصنام is a direct object of نعبد. (رَبِّ إِنَّهُنَّ أَضْلَلْنَ كَثِيراً مِنَ النَّاسِ): رب is a vocative with the vocative particle omitted, and a parallel has preceded; إن and its noun, and the clause أضللن is the predicate of إن; the pronoun refers to the idols, and what is meant by the supplication is asking for steadfastness and continuance in that; كثيرا is a direct object; ومن الناس is an adjective of كثيرا; and the clause إنهن is causal for His words واجنبني. (فَمَنْ تَبِعَنِي فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي): The fāʾ is a conjunction; من is a conditional noun that jusses, a mubtadaʾ; تبعني is a past verb in the position of jussive as the protasis, the nūn is protective and the yāʾ is the object; فإنه: the fāʾ is the linking fāʾ of the apodosis; إن and its noun; مني is its predicate; the clause is in the position of jussive as the apodosis; and the verb and its apodosis are the khabar of من.
(وَمَنْ عَصانِي فَإِنَّكَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ): A clause conjoined to its counterpart. (رَبَّنا إِنِّي أَسْكَنْتُ مِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِي بِوادٍ غَيْرِ ذِي زَرْعٍ عِنْدَ بَيْتِكَ الْمُحَرَّمِ): The vocative is repeated to stress earnest entreaty and humble supplication; إن and its noun, and the clause أسكنت is its predicate; ومن ذريتي is attached to something omitted as an adjective of the omitted object of أسكنت, meaning "I settled a progeny from my progeny," and من is partitive; بواد is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أسكنت; غير is an adjective of واد; ذي is annexed to غير and زرع to ذي; the adverbial عند بيتك is an adjective of واد; and المحرم is an adjective of بيتك. The details of this settling will come in the section on Benefits. (رَبَّنا لِيُقِيمُوا الصَّلاةَ): He repeated the vocative "Our Lord" to stress the entreaty. وليقيموا: the lām is the lām of cause and is attached to أسكنت, meaning "I settled them in this empty valley, barren of every convenience and provision, that they may establish the prayer at Your sacred House," that is, the House of great sanctity, "and inhabit it with Your remembrance and worship." (فَاجْعَلْ أَفْئِدَةً مِنَ النَّاسِ تَهْوِي إِلَيْهِمْ): The fāʾ is the eloquent fāʾ; واجعل أفئدة: a verb of supplication and a direct object; ومن الناس is an adjective of أفئدة, meaning "hearts"; the clause تهوي is the second direct object of اجعل; and إليهم is attached to تهوي. (وَارْزُقْهُمْ مِنَ الثَّمَراتِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَشْكُرُونَ): وارزقهم is conjoined to اجعل; ومن الثمرات is attached to ارزقهم, meaning "some of the fruits," so من is partitive; لعل and its noun; and the clause يشكرون is its predicate. (رَبَّنا إِنَّكَ تَعْلَمُ ما نُخْفِي وَما نُعْلِنُ): The repetition of the vocative is for repetition of the entreaty, and is evidence of humble supplication and taking refuge with Allah the Exalted. إن and its noun, and the clause تعلم is its predicate; ما is the object of تعلم; the clause نخفي is the ṣila; and وما نعلن is conjoined to ما نخفي. (وَما يَخْفى عَلَى اللَّهِ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلا فِي السَّماءِ): It may be from the speech of Allah the Exalted, confirming Ibrāhīm, or from the speech of Ibrāhīm. ما is negative; يخفى is an imperfect verb; على الله is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يخفى; من is redundant; شيء is genitive by من in form and agent in position; في الأرض is an adjective of شيء; and ولا في السماء is conjoined to في الأرض. (الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي وَهَبَ لِي عَلَى الْكِبَرِ إِسْماعِيلَ وَإِسْحاقَ): الحمد is a mubtadaʾ and لله the khabar; الذي is an adjective of لله; the clause وهب is the ṣila; لي is attached to وهب; على الكبر is in the position of accusative as a ḥāl, and على means "with" (maʿa), as in the verse of the poet:
إني على ما ترين من كبري ... أعلم من حيث تؤكل الكتف
("Despite my old age, as you see, I know from where the shoulder is eaten.")
وإسماعيل is a direct object and واسحق is conjoined to it. (إِنَّ رَبِّي لَسَمِيعُ الدُّعاءِ): إن and its noun; the shifted lām; and سميع الدعاء is its predicate; and the clause is a justification of His words وهب لي على الكبر. (رَبِّ اجْعَلْنِي مُقِيمَ الصَّلاةِ): اجعلني is a verb of supplication, the yāʾ is its first object and مقيم الصلاة its second object, meaning "one who continues in it."
(وَمِنْ ذُرِّيَّتِي رَبَّنا وَتَقَبَّلْ دُعاءِ): ومن ذريتي is conjoined to the yāʾ of the first-person speaker, meaning "and make some of my progeny establishers of the prayer," and this preposition phrase is in truth an adjective of that omitted object, meaning "and some from my progeny"; ربنا is a vocative; وتقبل is conjoined to what preceded; and دعائي is a direct object, and the yāʾ was dropped out of regard for the verse endings. (رَبَّنَا اغْفِرْ لِي وَلِوالِدَيَّ وَلِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الْحِسابُ): اغفر is a verb of supplication; لي is attached to اغفر; ولوالدي and وللمؤمنين are conjoined to لي; and يوم is an adverbial of time attached to something omitted as a ḥāl, meaning "the forgiveness being on that grievous day." More discussion on "the standing of the reckoning" will come in the section on Rhetoric.

* Rhetoric:
These verses are a magnificent collection of supplications in whose contemplations the soul of the believer is immersed and in whose beautiful turmoil it melts, and they contain a group of rhetorical arts that we summarise below:
1- Intellectual metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī) in attributing misguidance to the idols, which are inanimate things, or an unrestricted figurative usage (majāz mursal) whose relation is causation, because they are the cause of misguidance.
2- Antithesis (ṭibāq) in several forms, as in the words of the Exalted «ربنا إنك تعلم ما نخفي وما نعلن» and «وما يخفى عليه من شيء في الأرض ولا في السماء».
3- Metaphor in His words «يوم يقوم الحساب», meaning "is established," borrowed from the standing of one who stands over a man, and the proof of it is their saying "the war stood on its leg" and the like. You may also make it an unrestricted figurative usage whose relation is locality (maḥalliyya), like «واسأل القرية» ("and ask the town").

* Benefits:
The story of Ibrāhīm's settling his progeny:
History relates that Hājar was a slave girl of Sārah, who gave her to Ibrāhīm, and she bore him Ismāʿīl. Sārah became jealous of the two, because she had never given birth, and she adjured him by Allah to remove her from her presence. So Allah the Exalted commanded him by revelation to move her to the land of Mecca. He came from Syria, set her down in Mecca and returned the same day. Hājar followed him and said: "Where are you going, leaving me in this valley, in which there is no human and nothing?" He did not turn. She said: "Did Allah command you to do this?" He said: "Yes." She said: "Then He will not let me be lost." Then she returned, and Ibrāhīm went on, then raised his hands to heaven and recited the supplications that Allah expressed in His magnificent verses. He left with her a pouch of dates and a waterskin of water. When the water ran out, she and her son became thirsty, and Jibrīl came and struck the place of Zamzam with his heel or his wing, and water came out, and she began to drink from it. They remained so until a tribe of Jurhum passed by them, going to Syria; they were thirsty and saw water with her. They said to her: "Do you permit us to stop with you?" She said: "Yes, but you have no right to the water." They said: "Yes," and sent for their families, and they settled with them. When Ismāʿīl grew up he learned Arabic from them, and he was the most precious of them [Translator's note: the source prints "أنفسهم" (themselves); "anfas" (most precious) seems intended] and the most admired by them, so they married him to a woman from among them, and his mother died after he married; and so on to the end of this story, which needs a creative pen to weave from it the immortal drama.

dervis-irab:1-4.t:
* I'rab:
(الر كِتابٌ أَنْزَلْناهُ إِلَيْكَ لِتُخْرِجَ النَّاسَ مِنَ الظُّلُماتِ إِلَى النُّورِ): الر has had its parsing given before; كتاب is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "this is a book"; the clause أنزلناه is an adjective, and إليك is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أنزلناه. The lām is the causal lām; تخرج is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied أن after the causal lām, and the agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; الناس is a direct object; ومن الظلمات is attached to تخرج, and إلى النور is also attached to تخرج. (بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِمْ إِلى صِراطِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ): بإذن is attached to an omitted ḥāl, that is, "while you are permitted by your Lord"; ربهم is a muḍāf ilayhi; إلى صراط is a badal of His saying إلى النور, by repeating the governing particle; العزيز is a muḍāf ilayhi and الحميد is an adjective. (اللَّهِ الَّذِي لَهُ ما فِي السَّماواتِ وَما فِي الْأَرْضِ): الله in the genitive is a badal or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition) of العزيز الحميد; it was also read in the nominative, as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "He is Allah, who is characterised by the possession of what is in the heavens and what is in the earth". الذي is its adjective, وله is a fronted khabar, ما is a postponed mubtadaʾ, and the clause is the ṣila of الذي; في السموات is the ṣila of ما, and ما في الأرض is conjoined to ما في السموات. [Translator's note: the source prints «خير» in «على أنه خير لمبتدأ محذوف»; this appears to be a misprint for «خبر» (khabar), and the sense is rendered accordingly.] (وَوَيْلٌ لِلْكافِرِينَ مِنْ عَذابٍ شَدِيدٍ): ويل is a mubtadaʾ; it is permitted to begin with it because the intent is a supplication against the unbelievers; further discussion of this word will come in the section on benefits. The clause is an invocation and has no grammatical position; وللكافرين is the khabar; ومن عذاب is an adjective of ويل, or the two are attached to ويل; on the first view من is explicative (bayāniyya) and on the second it is for transitivity. شديد is an adjective. In the commentary of Abū l-Suʿūd: «ومن عذاب شديد» is attached to ويل in the sense that they wail and cry out from it, saying "O my woe!", as in His saying «دعوا هنالك ثبورا». Abū Ḥayyān forbade attaching it to ويل, saying: "«ومن عذاب شديد» is in the position of an adjective of ويل, and separation between the adjective and the described by the khabar does no harm; and it cannot be attached to ويل because it is a maṣdar, and it is not permissible to separate a maṣdar from what is attached to it by the khabar." [Translator's note: the closing quotation mark of Abū Ḥayyān's statement is missing in the source.] (الَّذِينَ يَسْتَحِبُّونَ الْحَياةَ الدُّنْيا عَلَى الْآخِرَةِ): الذين is an adjective of الكافرين, or a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the following clause أولئك في ضلال بعيد, or the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "they are those who prefer"; all these views are equal in preferability, which is why we have mentioned them. The clause يستحبون is a ṣila, الحياة is a direct object, الدنيا is an adjective, and على الآخرة is attached to يستحبون, because it is in the sense of preferring and choosing; it is the form istafʿala from love (maḥabba), because one who prefers a thing over another is as though he asks of himself that it be more beloved to it and more excellent in its sight than the other.
(وَيَصُدُّونَ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ وَيَبْغُونَها عِوَجاً): ويصدون is conjoined to يستحبون; عن سبيل الله is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يصدون; ويبغونها is conjoined to يصدون; يبغون is a verb and agent, and the hāʾ is accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, "they seek for it"; عوجا is a direct object. (أُولئِكَ فِي ضَلالٍ بَعِيدٍ): The demonstrative is a mubtadaʾ, في ضلال is its khabar, and بعيد is an adjective of ضلال. In making ضلال an adverbial container there is a rhetorical art to which we shall turn in the section on rhetoric. (وَما أَرْسَلْنا مِنْ رَسُولٍ إِلَّا بِلِسانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ): The wāw is resumptive, and the clause is resumptive, to explain the means of address which each messenger undertakes for his community. ما is negative, أرسلنا is a verb and agent, من is redundant, and رسول is genitive in form and accusative in position as an object; إلا is a particle of restriction; بلسان قومه is a ḥāl, that is, "bound up with the tongue of his people", so it is an exception from the most general of circumstances. ليبين: the lām is causal, and يبين is an imperfect verb in the subjunctive by an implied أن after the causal lām; ولهم is attached to يبين. (فَيُضِلُّ اللَّهُ مَنْ يَشاءُ وَيَهْدِي مَنْ يَشاءُ): The fāʾ is resumptive, and يضل is nominative as a new beginning; it is not permissible to conjoin it to يبين, as might be imagined, because the conjoined is like the conjoined-to in meaning, and the messengers were sent for clarification, not for leading astray. Al-Farrāʾ said: when a verb is mentioned and another verb after it, if the sequence is not similar to the first, then the nominative as a new beginning is the proper view; while al-Zajjāj said: "And if it were read in the accusative, taking the lām as the lām of consequence, it would be permissible." يضل الله is an imperfect verb and agent, من is a direct object, يشاء is a ṣila, and ويهدي من يشاء is conjoined to يضل الله من يشاء. (وَهُوَ الْعَزِيزُ الْحَكِيمُ): هو is a mubtadaʾ, العزيز is a first khabar, and الحكيم is a second khabar.

* Rhetoric:
These four verses contain several arts of rhetoric, which we summarise as follows:
1- «الظلمات» and «النور» are two explicit metaphors (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya) for error and guidance. Their like has been given before, so there is no need to repeat it.
2- In attributing remoteness to error there is a rational figurative usage (majāz ʿaqlī), because remoteness in reality belongs to the one who errs, since he is the one who strays far from the road; so his action is described by it, as you say "his good fortune is fortunate" and "a calamity calamitous".
3- In making error a container (ẓarf) there is also a figurative usage, as if it had encompassed them and clothed them in its blackness, so that they are plunged in it up to the chins, stumbling in its wildernesses and wandering aimlessly in its darknesses.
4- In making the "tongue" mean language there is a figurative usage whose relation is causality, because the tongue is the instrument of speech, for the meaning of «بلسان قومه» is "in the language of his people"; al-lisn and al-lisān are like al-rīsh and al-riyāsh (plumage). A detailed account of the language of the Qur'an and of the seven dialects in which it was read will come in the section on benefits. The word lisān was put in the singular because what is meant is language. An difficulty has been raised about this verse, because the Prophet ﷺ was sent to all people, whose languages differ and whose tongues vary. The answer is that although he ﷺ was sent to all mankind, since his people were the Arabs and they were more particular to him and nearer to him, his being sent in their tongue was preferable to his being sent in the tongue of others; they explain it to those whose tongue is different from theirs and make it clear to them until they understand it as they themselves understand it. Had the Qur'an been sent down in all the languages of those to whom he was sent, and had the Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained it to each people in their tongue, that would have been a likely cause of disagreement and would have opened wide the door of dispute, because every community might claim, for meanings in its tongue, what others do not know; and it might also have led to alteration and distortion by reason of the false claims into which the partisans would fall.
5- Antithesis (ṭibāq) between يضل and يهدي. All these arts have been discussed in their proper places.

* Benefits:
The benefits in these verses are enough to fill volumes, but following the method of the book we shall confine ourselves to what must be mentioned, as follows:

1- (وَيْلٌ):
A word of threat and menace; it is the opposite of waʾl, that is, safety; a noun meaning destruction, except that no verb is derived from it; one says only waylan lahu, in the accusative as maṣdars are, and then it is made nominative, like them, to convey the sense of permanence, so one says waylun lahu, like salāmun ʿalayka. In al-Mukhtār: al-wāʾil is the refuge, and waʾala ilayhi means he took refuge in it; its pattern is that of waʿada, and its maṣdar is waʾūl on the pattern of wujūd. Waylu Zaydin and wayḥuhu are both accusative as maṣdars. It was said: wayl is a word of punishment, and wayḥ a word of compassion.

2- The language of the Qur'an and the opinion of Dr. Ṭāhā Ḥusayn:
The language of the Qur'an:
It is a self-standing science, and it appears that the noble ḥadīth «نزل القرآن على سبعة أحرف» ("the Qur'an was sent down in seven aḥruf") was a cause of the rise of this science among the sciences of the Qur'an. The most recent and most sound of the studies on it is what Dr. Ṭāhā Ḥusayn determined in his book al-Adab al-Jāhilī, and the following is a summary of this valuable discussion. Dr. Ṭāhā establishes that there is a fundamental difference between the language that people used in the south of the Arab lands and the language they used in the north of these lands; and from establishing this he comes to the conclusion that the early and late scholars are confused in defining what should be understood by the word "Arabs" and what should be understood by the term "the Arabic language", and that this confusion is not of a kind to help scholarly investigation. Then the professor goes on to mention the differences between the language of the southern Arabs and that of the northern Arabs, and cites some texts discovered by Professor Guidi from the Ḥimyarite language, and how it differs very greatly from the Ḥijāzī Qurashī language that we know. An example is this text, which says: «وهبم واخهو بنو كلبت هقنيو إلى مقه ذهرن ذن فرندن حجن وقههمو بمسألهو لو فيهمو وسعدهمو نعمتم», of which the meaning is: "Wahab (the name of a man) and his brother, the sons of Kalbat, dedicated to Maqqah (the name of a god in Hurān) this tablet, because he answered them in their petition, kept them safe and helped them with his favour." He goes on in this long discussion until he says: "The Qur'an, which was recited in a single language and a single dialect, that of Quraysh and its dialect, had hardly been taken up by the reciters from the various tribes when its readings multiplied, the dialects in it were many and differed greatly, which perplexed the later reciters and scholars in fixing and verifying it, and they set up for it a special science or sciences. We are not referring here to those readings which differ greatly among themselves in the fixing of vowels, whether the vowel be one of structure or one of inflection (iʿrāb); we are not referring to the readers' disagreement in putting al-ṭayr in the accusative or the nominative in the verse «يا جبال أوّبي معه والطير», nor to their disagreement in putting damma or fatḥa on the fāʾ in the verse «لقد جاءكم رسول من أنفسكم». We refer only to another kind of difference in the readings, which reason accepts and transmission allows, and which is required by the necessary difference of dialects among the Arab tribes, who could not change their throats, tongues and lips to recite the Qur'an as the Prophet and his clan of Quraysh recited it, so they recited it as they spoke: they used imāla where they did not use imāla, shortened where they did not shorten, put sukūn where they did not put sukūn, and assimilated, or concealed, or transferred where they did not assimilate, conceal or transfer."

A pause that is necessary:
Here is a pause that cannot be avoided. Some men of religion understood these seven readings to be mutawātir from the Prophet, brought down by Gabriel upon his heart, so that whoever denies them is an unbeliever without any doubt or suspicion, and they found no proof to rely on for what they say except what is narrated in the Ṣaḥīḥ, that he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "The Qur'an was sent down in seven aḥruf". The truth is that these seven readings are not from revelation in little or much, and whoever denies them is neither an unbeliever nor a sinner nor impugned in his religion; they are only readings whose source is the dialects and their differences. People may argue about them, reject some and accept others; they have in fact argued about them and disputed, and some have declared others wrong in them, and we know of no Muslim who declared another an unbeliever for any of this. These readings are not the seven aḥruf in which the Qur'an was sent down; they are one thing and those aḥruf another. For aḥruf is the plural of ḥarf, and ḥarf is language; so the meaning of "the Qur'an was sent down in seven aḥruf" is that it was sent down in seven languages differing in their wording and substance. This is explained by the saying of Ibn Masʿūd: "It is only like your saying halumma, taʿāla and aqbil" (all meaning "come"). It is explained by the saying of Anas on the verse «إن ناشئة الليل هي أشد وطئا وأصوب قيلا»: "aṣwab, aqwam and ahdā are one"; and by the reading of Ibn Masʿūd «ما ينظرون إلا زقية واحدة» in place of «ما ينظرون إلا صيحة واحدة».
The aḥruf are other than the readings:
The aḥruf are therefore the languages that differ among themselves in wording and substance. As for these readings, which differ in shortening and lengthening, in vowel and sukūn, in transfer and retention, and in the vowels of inflection, they are not among the aḥruf at all, because they are a difference in form and shape, not in substance and wording. The Muslims have agreed that the Qur'an was sent down in seven aḥruf, that is, in seven languages differing in their words and substance, and the Muslims have agreed that the Companions of the Prophet disputed about these seven aḥruf, each reciting according to the ḥarf he had heard from the Prophet, and the disagreement and dispute over this grew severe until strife almost occurred among the people, especially in the armies of the Muslims who were raiding and holding the frontier posts, far from the place of descent of the revelation and the seat of the caliphate. The matter was raised to the caliph ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, who was alarmed by it and feared for the Muslims that there might befall them what befell the Christians in their disagreement over the text of the Gospel, as they differed over the text of the Injīl. So he collected the muṣḥaf for them and circulated it in the garrison cities, and ordered that the other copies be wiped out completely. On this basis the six aḥruf were wiped out and only one ḥarf remained, which is the ḥarf that we read in the muṣḥaf of ʿUthmān, the ḥarf of Quraysh, and that is the ḥarf in which the dialects of the reciters differed: some lengthened and some shortened, one group pronounced heavily and another lightly, one group transferred and another retained. Then Dr. Ṭāhā cited what is in the first volume of the Tafsīr of Ibn Jarīr al-Ṭabarī in support of his opinion.

Summary of al-Ṭabarī's statement:
Ibn Jarīr said, in summary: some scholars held that the seven aḥruf are seven meanings, namely command, prohibition, promise, threat, disputation, narrative and parable. But he opposes this and says: the seven aḥruf are seven languages from the languages of clans of the Arab tribes with differing tongues. He mentioned that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah disputed over the recitation of part of the Qur'an, differing in its reading but not in its interpretation, and some denied the reading of others, each reader claiming that the Messenger of Allah had made him recite what he recited in the manner in which he recited; then they took the matter to the Messenger of Allah, and it was among the Messenger's judgements between them that he declared each reader's recitation correct, even though it differed from the recitation of his companions who disputed with him, and he commanded each man to recite as he had been taught, until doubt about Islam entered the heart of some of them when he saw the Messenger's endorsing the recitation of each despite their difference; then Allah dispelled it through the Messenger's explanation to him that the Qur'an is in seven aḥruf.
Al-Ṭabarī then took up an important point, which is the reply to the questioners:
"What is the matter with the other six aḥruf that they are not found, when the Messenger of Allah made his Companions recite them and commanded recitation in them and Allah sent them down from Himself to His Prophet? Were they abrogated and removed? What is the evidence of their abrogation and removal? Or did the community forget them, in which case that is a neglect of what they were commanded to preserve? Or what is the story?" Ibn Jarīr gave a masterly answer to these awkward questions, saying: The six aḥruf were not abrogated and removed, nor did the community neglect them while commanded to preserve them; rather the community was commanded to preserve the Qur'an and given the choice to recite and preserve it in whichever of those seven aḥruf it wished. He gave an example from jurisprudence: if a wealthy man breaks an oath, he may choose one of three expiations: either emancipation, or feeding, or clothing. So likewise the community was commanded to preserve and recite the Qur'an and was given the choice to recite it in whichever of the seven aḥruf it wished. And for some reason, it became obligatory upon it to adhere to one ḥarf, reciting in one ḥarf and abandoning recitation in the remaining six aḥruf, without the reader being forbidden from reciting it in all its aḥruf as he was permitted to recite it.
The opinion of al-Suyūṭī in al-Itqān:
As for al-Suyūṭī, in his book al-Itqān he affirmed the soundness of the ḥadīth on the testimony of twenty-one Companions whom he named; then ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān wished to ascertain its soundness, so he asked the Muslims, who were gathered in the mosque, that whoever had heard this ḥadīth should stand, and all who were in the mosque stood. He said: "And I testify with them." Al-Suyūṭī moved on to discussing the opinions said about this ḥadīth, and they came to about forty opinions. He began by adding a problem to the problems already existing in this topic, saying: the number seven is not meant literally; rather what is meant is ease, facility and breadth, and the word "seven" is used to mean multitude among the units, as "seventy" is used among the tens. But he rejected this opinion because there are many verses in the Qur'an that are read in more than seven ways, and some that are read in fewer, and some whose vowelling changed but whose meaning and form (the substance of the word) did not change; and among them is what al-Ṭabarī mentioned of a difference of words with agreement of meanings. Al-Ṭaḥāwī mentioned that this was a concession when it was hard for many of them to recite in a single wording, owing to their ignorance of writing, vowelling and mastery of script, and that it was then abrogated when the excuse disappeared and writing and memorisation became easy. He gave as an example of this that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd was teaching a man the Qur'an and recited to him «طَعامُ الْأَثِيمِ», and the man said "ṭaʿām al-yathīm"; he made him repeat it, but his tongue would not manage it, so he said: "Can you say ṭaʿām al-fājir?" He said: Yes. He said: "Then do so."
Another opinion, held by many scholars such as Abū ʿUbayd, Thaʿlab and al-Zuhrī, is that the seven aḥruf are seven languages. When it was said to them that the languages of the Arabs are more than seven, they answered that what is meant is the most eloquent of them.
Abū ʿUbayd has a valuable opinion, that there are in the Qur'an seven languages scattered in it, some in the language of Quraysh, some in the language of Hudhayl, some in the language of Hawāzin, some in the language of Yemen and others; that is, there are words and phrases in the Qur'an that were known to this tribe and that tribe.
Al-Suyūṭī went on to present another group of opinions of no importance, then ended his discussion by saying: "Many of the common people think that what is meant by the seven aḥruf is the seven readings, and this is hideous ignorance."

A sufficient summary:
The discussion would be long if we went on tracing what has been said on this matter or investigating the origins from which the Arabic language extends; the reader can refer to them in the books written on the subject, and it is enough for us to say now: the Qur'an was sent down in the Qurashī Arabic language, in which the other languages dissolved, and especially the languages of the neighbouring tribes. The Companions understood the Qur'an in general, but not a few words were obscure to them, and indeed some of them remain obscure to us today, despite the fact that the means of knowing some ancient languages are now available to us. It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb did not understand the word «أبا» in «وفاكهة وأبا», and he is excused, for it is an Abyssinian word. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that two bedouins disputed before him over a well, and one of them said: "I originated it (anā faṭartuhā)", and the other opposed him. Ibn ʿAbbās said:
"Then I understood the meaning of His saying «فاطر السموات والأرض»." It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he did not understand the meaning of the verse «ربنا افتح بيننا وبين قومنا بالحق» until he heard a girl of Yemen (the daughter of Dhū Yazan) calling her husband:
"Anā taḥik", meaning "I shall litigate with you."
Ibn al-Naqīb mentioned in Khaṣāʾiṣ al-Qurʾān that the Qur'an contains all the languages of the Arabs, and that a great deal of the languages of others, of the Romans, Persians and Abyssinians, was sent down in it. We have already cited this statement. Among the non-Arabic words whose presence in the Qur'an the ancients noted are the following:
[Translator's note: the list below is printed in the source in a garbled order, with stray markers «ل 1» and «ل 2» and a broken line; it is translated as printed, and the attributions are the author's.]
istabraq: Greek; ibliʿī māʾaki: Indian or Abyssinian; al-arāʾik: Abyssinian; iṣr (that is, covenant): Nabataean; awwāb: "the Messiah" in Abyssinian; baṭāʾinuhā (that is, its outsides): in Coptic; tannūr: Persian; jahannam: Greek or Persian; ḥawāriyyūn (that is, washers): in Abyssinian; durriyy (that is, shining): in Abyssinian; al-sijill: the book, in Abyssinian; al-rass (that is, the well): in Greek; sariyy: said to be Syriac or Nabataean or Greek; al-ṣirāṭ: the road, in the language of the Romans; ʿadn: the vines, in Syriac; ghīḍa (that is, decreased): in Abyssinian; al-qisṭ: justice, in Persian; qaswara: the lion, in Abyssinian; kiflayn: double, in Abyssinian; mishkāt: the niche, in Abyssinian; minsaʾa: a staff, in Nabataean; ab: Abyssinian; akhlada: Hebrew; asfār: Syriac or Nabataean; alīm: "painful"; they said it is Zanji or Hebrew; al-adāt: "the one who is certain", in Abyssinian; ḥaṣab: in the sense of "firewood" in Zanji; dīnār: Persian; rahwan: "easy", in Syriac; sijjīl: Persian; sundus: Persian and Indian; al-ṭāghūt: the soothsayer, in Abyssinian; ghassāq: "the stinking cold", in Turkish; al-firdaws: the garden, in Greek; al-qisṭās: the scale, in Persian; kāfūr: in Persian; al-yamm: the sea, in Syriac and Coptic; nāshiʾat al-layl: in Abyssinian; wizr: the refuge, in Nabataean; kuwwirat (that is, ghuwwirat): in Persian; marqūm: "written", in Arabic; manāṣ: flight, in Nabataean; al-muhl: oil, in the tongue of the Berbers; hawnan: in Syriac; hayta lak: in Coptic; yāqūt: in Persian; yaḥūr: "returns", in Abyssinian; yaʿhad (that is, ripens): in Berber; al-fūm: wheat, in Hebrew. Al-Suyūṭī cited these words and others in al-Itqān, as he cited hundreds of words that occur in the Qur'an in a language other than that of the Ḥijāz, among them languages of Yemen. He stated explicitly many Ḥimyarite words in particular; he mentioned, for example, that asṭūr in the language of Ḥimyar means "book", and on this basis His saying «وكتاب مسطور» is understood; and he mentioned that al-lahw means "woman" in the language of Yemen, and on this basis the verse «لو أردنا أن نتخذ لهوا» is understood. What, we ask, prevents it, given that it is established for us that of the Qur'anic words and the many sources from which they came, the seven aḥruf are these many languages that dissolved into the language of Quraysh, some of which the Prophet knew, and which the words of the Qur'an included?
We incline in principle, though we have no means of final certainty, to hold that this is the correct view regarding the seven aḥruf: they point to many words from several languages used by the Qur'an, among them Persian, Greek, Aramaic, Chaldean, Abyssinian, Ḥimyarite, Hebrew, Syriac and Egyptian, all of which were added to the language of Quraysh, strengthening its standing and removing the weakness and poverty that existed in the language of the other tribes who used to come on pilgrimage, which insist on certain letters in place of others, such as replacing the feminine kāf with shīn, so that they say kitābush for kitābuki, and on this is based his saying:
فعيناش عيناها وجيدش جيدها ... ولكن عظم الساق منش دقيق
(Her eyes are her eyes and her neck her neck, but the bone of the shin on you is thin.)
and its original is:
فعيناك عيناها وجيدك جيدها ... ولكن عظم الساق منك دقيق
This is the tribe of Qays. Likewise those who cannot pronounce the sīn and replace it with tāʾ, so that for them al-nās is al-nāt; these are the tribe of Tamīm.
The Qur'an was free of these many dialects and kept to inflection (iʿrāb) at the ends of all words, which was not kept in many of the other languages. The Prophet, as the recipient of revelation and the first teacher of the Qur'an, knew the interpretation of everything that was sent down to him, and what his Companions asked him about he told them; perhaps they avoided asking him about many words, as is shown by their ignorance of them after his death and their being forbidden to strain and probe, that is, to search into the meaning of every word and dig behind it. What we say here, that the seven aḥruf concern the words of the Qur'an, is not an odd statement that nobody made; many have said it, among them Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām, Thaʿlab, Abū Ḥātim al-Sijistānī and others.
Therefore it is wholly wrong to say that a Qur'an was sent down to be the miracle of a prophet and then to say: we are able to put one word in place of another because we have many words, that is, synonyms. Listen to this verse: «للذين آمنوا انظرونا», and then we read it according to the aḥruf of which they speak, thus: «للذين آمنوا امهلونا» or «للذين آمنوا ارقبونا». Let us leave it to the reader to examine a little and think at length, to see whether the meaning of all these expressions agrees and whether they keep their place in inimitability in this form. And listen to another verse:
«كلما أضاء لهم مشوا فيه» and «كلما أضاء لهم مروا فيه» and «كلما أضاء لهم سعوا فيه»: whoever says that mashā, saʿā and marra are equal in usage is wholly ignorant, groping blindly in error.
The seven aḥruf, then, are something other than these alterations and substitutions, and the nearest to the truth in explaining them is what we mentioned, that the Qur'an contains many foreign words which entered it and the language of Quraysh from the peoples surrounding the peninsula. More explanation of this noble discussion will come; it has run somewhat long and was not a condition of the book.
On this occasion we recall that the late Professor ʿAbbās Maḥmūd al-ʿAqqād wrote his two books «Abū l-Anbiyāʾ: al-Khalīl Ibrāhīm» and «al-Thaqāfa al-ʿArabiyya asbaq min thaqāfat al-Yūnān wa-l-ʿIbriyyīn», in which he took up the question of the language of the Friend of the Merciful, Abraham, upon him be blessings and peace, and replied to the deviants who wish to steer their research in a particular direction, preceded by a plan by which the Arabs would be severed from their connection with the Friend, and he established Abraham's close connection with Arabness at an early time falling between the nineteenth and eighteenth centuries before the Christian era. To complete his lofty study we see fit to cite a ḥadīth narrated by Imam al-Bukhārī in his Ṣaḥīḥ, which he reported with his chain from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both. This ḥadīth took up several pages of this great work; we summarise it and delimit its topics as follows:
1- It speaks of the pure persons who settled in Mecca at a time when no one was there and no water: the Friend Abraham, Hagar and her nursing son Ishmael.
2- The gushing forth of Zamzam for Hagar and her son.
3- The arrival of an Arab clan of Jurhum and their asking Hagar's permission to settle in Mecca, accepting her condition "that they have no right to the water"; they brought their families, and Ishmael, upon him be peace, grew up among them and married from them twice.
4- Three visits of the Friend to Mecca to see his charge, besides the first, in which he came to it with his family; the last of them was that visit with his son, and he was commanded to proclaim the pilgrimage among the people.
This ḥadīth gives important objective facts that clarify some of what history, in its modern method, has missed.
The first: its clear statement of the beginning of the history of settlement in Mecca.
The second: it clarifies a missing link, for historians, about the kingdoms of the Ishmaelites in the north of the Arabian Peninsula.
The third: the language of the Friend. For the Friend visited Mecca four times, and Ishmael married two women of Jurhum and spoke and conversed with them in Arabic necessarily, without an interpreter; so what al-ʿAqqād said is sound. We do not say that he spoke the Arabic which is our Arabic, I mean the language of the Noble Qur'an, but the Arabic of his time, closely connected in roots and branches with the Arabic of the Noble Qur'an.

farraa:1-2.t: The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ ٱلْعَزِيزِ ٱلْحَمِيدِ﴾ ﴿ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِي﴾ ("to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy — Allah, to whom…"). [الله] is made genitive in i'rab and nominative. The genitive is by making it follow (الحَمِيدِ), and the nominative is by resumption (istiʾnāf), because it is separated from the verse [before it]; as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿إِنَّ اللهَ اشْتَرَى مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ أَنْفُسَهُمْ وَأَمْوَالَهُمْ بأَنَّ لَهُمُ الجَنَّةَ﴾ ("Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth in exchange for the Garden being theirs") to the end of the verse, after which He said: ﴿التَّائِبُونَ﴾ ("those who repent"), while in the reading of ʿAbdullāh [Ibn Masʿūd] it is (التائِبين). All of that is correct.

farraa:4-4.t:
His saying: ﴿وَمَآ أَرْسَلْنَا مِن رَّسُولٍ إِلاَّ بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ لِيُبَيِّنَ لَهُمْ﴾ ("We have not sent any messenger except in the tongue of his people, that he might make things clear to them"). He is saying: that he might make them understand and the proof be binding upon them. Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿فَيُضِلُّ ٱللَّهُ مَن يَشَآءُ﴾ ("then Allah leads astray whom He wills"), putting it in the nominative because the intention in it is resumption (istiʾnāf), not conjunction with what precedes it. Similar to it is ﴿لِنُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ وَنُقِرُّ فىِ الأَرْحَامِ مَا نشَاءُ﴾ ("that We may make clear to you; and We settle in the wombs whom We will"), and similar to it in Barāʾa: ﴿قَاتِلُوهُمْ يَعَذِّبْهُمُ اللهُ بِأَيْدِكُمْ﴾ ("fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands"), after which He said: ﴿وَيَتُوبُ اللهُ عَلَى مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ ("and Allah turns in mercy to whom He wills"). So when you see a verb in the accusative followed by a verb coordinated to it with wāw, fāʾ, thumma or aw: if it matches the meaning of the verb before it, coordinate it with it; and if you see that it does not match its meaning, take it as a fresh start and put it in the nominative.
Of the cut-off kind is what I have told you. Also of it is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَاللهُ يُرِيدُ أَنْ يَتُوبَ عَلَيْكُم وَيُرِيدُ الَّذِينَ يَتَّبِعُون الشَّهَوَاتِ﴾ ("Allah wishes to turn to you in mercy, and those who follow their desires wish…"). You make (ويريد الذين) nominative because it does not match (أَنْ يَتُوبَ) — do you not see that joining the two is not permissible? — so you resume, or refer it back to His saying ﴿وَاللهُ يُرِيدُ﴾. Similar to it is ﴿يُرِيدُونَ أَنْ يُطْفِئُوا نُورَ اللهِ بِأَفْوَاهِهِمْ وَيَأْبَى اللهُ إِلاَّ أَنْ يُتِمَّ نُورَهُ﴾ ("they wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light"): yaʾbā is in the position of the nominative; nothing else is permissible.
Similar to it is his saying:

والشعر لا يَسْطيعُه من يظلمه * يريد أن يعربه فيُعجِمُه
(Poetry is beyond the one who wrongs it: he wishes to make it clear, and so he garbles it.)

Likewise you say: "I come to you if you come to me, and I honour you (wa-ukrimaka)", referring "I honour you" back to the first verb because it matches it; and you say: "I come to you if you come to me and do good to me (wa-tuḥsina)", referring "and do good" back to what matches it. Analogies are drawn on this.

farraa:5-5.t: His saying: ﴿وَذَكِّرْهُمْ بِأَيَّامِ ٱللَّهِ﴾ ("and remind them of the days of Allah"). He is saying: make them fear, by the days of ʿĀd, Thamūd and their like, with punishment, and with pardon for others. In meaning it is like your saying: "Take them with severity and gentleness."

farraa:6-6.t:
His saying here: ﴿وَيُذَبِّحُونَ﴾ ("and they slaughter"), while in another place it is ﴿يُذَبِّحُونَ﴾ without wāw, and in another place ﴿يُقَتِّلُونَ﴾ ("they kill") without wāw. The meaning of the wāw is that a punishment other than slaughter touched them, as though He said: "they punish you with other than slaughter and with slaughter". The meaning of dropping the wāw is as though it were an explanation of the kinds of punishment. When a report of punishment or reward is given summarily in one word and you then explain it, put it without wāw; and when its first part is other than its last, then with wāw. Of the summary kind is the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿وَمَنْ يَفْعَلْ ذَلِكَ يَلْقَ أَثَاماً﴾ ("whoever does that will meet a penalty"): al-athām there carries the intention of punishment, little and much. Then He explained it without wāw, saying: ﴿يُضاعَفْ لَهُ العَذَابُ يَوْمَ القِيَامَةِ﴾ ("the punishment will be doubled for him on the Day of Resurrection"). Were it not summary, what is not of it would not be an explanation of it. Do you not see that you say: "I have two mounts, a mule and a work-horse", whereas it is not permissible to say "I have two mounts, and a mule and a work-horse" when you mean to explain the two mounts as the mule and the work-horse? In this there is sufficiency for what we leave out of that, so draw analogies on it.
His saying: ﴿وَفِي ذٰلِكُمْ بَلاۤءٌ مِّن رَّبَّكُمْ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("and in that was a great trial from your Lord"). He is saying: in the kinds of punishment that Pharaoh used to inflict on you there was a great balāʾ, in the sense of affliction. And it is said: in that were great favours from your Lord, since He saved you from it. Balāʾ can be favours and it can be punishment. Do you not see that you say: "So-and-so has done you good balāʾ", meaning his bestowing favour on you?

farraa:7-7.t: His saying: ﴿وَإِذْ تَأَذَّنَ رَبُّكُمْ﴾ ("and when your Lord proclaimed"): its meaning is "your Lord made known". The Arabs sometimes say tafaʿʿaltu in the sense of afʿaltu, and this is of that — and Allah knows best: awʿadanī and tawaʿʿadanī ("he threatened me"); and it is frequent.

farraa:9-9.t:
His saying: ﴿فَرَدُّوۤاْ أَيْدِيَهُمْ فِيۤ أَفْوَاهِهِمْ﴾ ("and they returned their hands to their mouths"). Several views have come about it. Muḥammad narrated to us, saying: al-Farrāʾ narrated to us, saying: Ḥibbān narrated to me from al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: when the messenger came to them they would say to him, "Be silent!" and point with their fingers to their own mouths, as you silence [someone] — he said: and al-Farrāʾ showed us, placing his index finger on his mouth — in rejection of them and giving them the lie. Some said: they used to give them the lie and push the speech back with their hands into the mouths of the messengers — and al-Farrāʾ showed us thus, with the back of his hand towards the person he was addressing. He said: and Ibn ʿAbdullāh showed us the gesture in both ways (and the shaykh Ibn al-ʿAbbās showed us the gesture in both ways). And some said: "so they returned their hands in their mouths" means: they rejected with their mouths what would have been, had they accepted it, favours and benefactions (ayādī) from Allah; "in their mouths" meaning "with their mouths", i.e. with their tongues. We have found among the Arabs some who put fī in the place of bāʾ, saying: "May Allah admit you bi-l-janna", meaning "into (fī) the Garden". He said: and one of them recited to me:

وأرغب فيها عن لَقِيطٍ ورهطه * ولكنّنى عن سِنْبِس لست أرغب
(And I hold her too dear for Laqīṭ and his clan, but from Sinbis I do not hold back.)

He said "arghabu fīhā", meaning a daughter of his, i.e. "I hold her too dear (arghabu bihā) for Laqīṭ".

farraa:13-13.t:
His saying: ﴿وَقَالَ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ لِرُسُلِهِمْ لَنُخْرِجَنَّـكُمْ مِّنْ أَرْضِنَآ أَوْ لَتَعُودُنَّ فِي مِلَّتِنَا﴾ ("and those who disbelieved said to their messengers: 'We will surely drive you out of our land, or you shall return to our religion'"). He said ﴿أَوْ لَتَعُودُنَّ﴾, putting a lām in it like the answer of an oath, while it is in the sense of a condition. Similar to it in speech is that you say: "By Allah, I will surely beat you, or you acknowledge [my right]", so that its meaning is the meaning of ḥattā ("until") or illā ("unless"), except that it came with a coordinating particle. Some Arabs make the condition follow what precedes it: if there is a lām in the first, there is a lām in the second; and if the first is accusative or jussive they coordinate [the second] with it, as in His saying ﴿أَوْ لَتَعُودُنَّ﴾. And some Arabs put what follows aw in the accusative, so that its accusative signals that it is cut off from what precedes it. The poet said:

لَتقعُدِنَّ مقعدَ القَصِىِّ * منِّىَ ذى القاذُورة المَقْلِىّ
أَو تحلفى بربّك العلىِّ * أنيِّ أبو ذيَّالِكِ الصبىّ
(You shall sit from me in the seat of the remote one, the filthy, the hated — unless you swear by your Lord, the Most High, that I am the father of that little boy.)

He put (تحلفى) in the accusative because he meant: "unless (an) you swear". Had he said "aw la-taḥlifinna" it would be correct. Similar to it is the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:

بكى صاحبى لَمَّا رأى الدرب دونه * وأيقن أنّا لاحقان بقَيْصَرا
فقلت له لا تبك عَيْنُك إنّما * نحاولُ مُلْكا أَو نموتَ فنُعذرا
(My companion wept when he saw the mountain pass before him and was certain that we were joining Caesar. I said to him: let your eye not weep; we only seek a kingdom — or else we die and are excused.)

He put the last [verb] in the accusative and made (نحاول) nominative, in the sense of illā or ḥattā. And in one of the two readings: ﴿تَقَاتِلُونَهُمْ أَوْ يُسْلِمُوا﴾ ("you will fight them unless they submit"), and the meaning — and Allah knows best — is: you will fight them until they submit. And the poet said:

لا أستطيع نُزوعاً عن مودّتها * أوْ يصنعَ الحبُّ بى غير الذى صَنَعَا
(I cannot desist from loving her, unless love does to me other than what it has done.)

And you say in speech: "I am not my father's son if I do not kill you, or you outrun me in the land (aw tasbiqanī / aw tasbiqnī)", putting tasbiqnī in the accusative or the jussive. The jussive is permissible as though: "I am not my father's son if one of these two does not happen"; the accusative is on the basis that its end is cut off from its beginning, as they said: "Nothing is too wide for me and yet too narrow for you (wa-yaḍīqa)" — it was not proper to carry lā over onto wa-yaḍīq, so it was known that it is cut off from its meaning. Likewise the saying of the Arabs: "Had you been left with the lion (wa-l-asada), it would have eaten you": since the wāw came to carry a noun over onto a noun before it, and it was ugly to carry the verb that made the first nominative over onto the second, [the second] became accusative — do you not see that you do not say: "Had you been left and the lion been left, it would have eaten you"? From here the accusative came to it. And the nominative is permissible because the wāw is a well-known coordinating particle; so both ways are permissible in it, for the two reasons.

farraa:14-14.t: His saying: ﴿ذٰلِكَ لِمَنْ خَافَ مَقَامِي﴾ ("that is for whoever fears My station"): its meaning is "that is for whoever fears his standing before Me". Similar to it is His saying: ﴿وَتَجْعَلُون رِزْقَكُمْ أَنَّكُمْ تُكَذِّبُونَ﴾ ("and you make your provision that you deny"), its meaning being: "My providing for you, that you deny". The Arabs annex their actions both to themselves and to what the action falls upon; they say: "I regretted my beating you" and "I regretted your beating", and this is of that — and Allah knows best.

farraa:17-17.t:
His saying: ﴿وَلاَ يَكَادُ يُسِيغُهُ﴾ ("and he can hardly swallow it"): yet he does swallow it. The Arabs use (لا يكاد) both for what has been done and for what has not been done. As for what has been done, it is clear here from that, because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says of what He made food for them: ﴿إِنَّ شَجَرّةَ الزَّقُّومِ طَعَامُ الأَثيمِ كالمُهْلِ يَغْلِى فى البُطُونِ﴾ ("the tree of al-Zaqqūm is the food of the sinner; like molten metal it boils in the bellies"); so this too is a punishment in their bellies which they swallow. As for where kāda enters and the thing is not done, it is your saying in speech: "I did not come to him, nor nearly", and the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, in al-Nūr: ﴿إِذَا أَخْرَجَ يَدَهُ لَمْ يَكَدْ يَراهَا﴾ ("when he puts out his hand he can hardly see it"). In our view — and Allah knows best — this means he does not see it. Some of the jurists have said that, because it is not seen in darknesses less than these, so how about darknesses described in the most extreme description?
His saying: ﴿وَيَأْتِيهِ ٱلْمَوْتُ مِن كُلِّ مَكَانٍ﴾ ("and death comes to him from every place"). Al-Farrāʾ narrated to us, saying: Ḥibbān narrated to me from al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: (يأتِيِه المَوْتُ) means: the punishment comes to him from before him and from behind him, from his right and from his left. Hushaym narrated to me from al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab, from Ibrāhīm al-Taymī, who said: from every hair.
His saying: ﴿وَمَا هُوَ بِمَيِّتٍ﴾ ("yet he is not dead"). When a thing has already died, the Arabs say mayt and mayyit. If they say "he is a dead man if you strike him", they say māʾit and mayyit. Some of the readers read ﴿إِنَّك مَائِتٌ وَإِنَّهُمْ مَائِتُون﴾ ("you will die and they will die"), while the reading of the generality is (ميّت). Likewise they say: "This is the lord (sayyid) of his people", and "he is not about to become their lord (sāʾid) shortly"; they say sāʾidahum and sayyidahum. They do likewise with every attribute, such as ṭamiʿ: one says ṭamiʿ when someone is characterised by greed, and one says "he is ṭāmiʿ (hoping) to get some good from you". They say "he is sakrān (drunk)" when he is in his drunkenness, and "he is not sākir [about to be drunk] from much drinking". And "he is karīm (generous)" when he is characterised by generosity; but if you intend a generosity that will come from him in the future, you say kārim.

farraa:18-18.t:
His saying: ﴿مَّثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ بِرَبِّهِمْ﴾ ("the likeness of those who disbelieve in their Lord"). He annexed "likeness" to them, then said: ﴿أَعْمَالُهُمْ كَرَمَادٍ ٱشْتَدَّتْ بِهِ ٱلرِّيحُ﴾ ("their deeds are like ashes on which the wind blows hard"), while the likeness is of the deeds. The Arabs do that. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿وَيَوْمَ القِيَامَةِ تَرَى الَّذِينَ كَذَبُوا عَلَى اللهِ وُجُوهُهُم مُسْوَدَّةٌ﴾ ("on the Day of Resurrection you will see those who lied about Allah, their faces blackened"), and the meaning is: you will see their faces blackened. That is good Arabic, because they find the meaning at the end of the expression and so do not mind what fell upon the first noun (al-ism al-mubtadaʾ). Also possible in it is to repeat on the second what fell on the first noun, as in His saying: ﴿لَجَعَلْنَا لِمَنْ يَكْفُرُ بِالرَّحْمَنِ لِبُيُوتِهِمْ سُقُفاً﴾ ("We would have made for whoever disbelieves in the All-Merciful, for their houses, roofs [of silver]"): the lām was repeated with "houses" because they are what is meant by the roofs. Had you used the genitive without making the lām overt it would be correct, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿يَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الشَّهْرِ الْحَرَامِ قِتَالٍ فيه﴾ ("they ask you about the sacred month — fighting in it").
